'''Jennifer Lippincott-Schwartz''' is a Senior Group Leader at [[Howard Hughes Medical Institute]]'s [[Janelia Research Campus]] and a founding member of the Neuronal Cell Biology Program at Janelia.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.hhmi.org/news/neuronal-cell-biology-research-program-added-janelia-research-campus|title=Neuronal Cell Biology Research Program Added at Janelia Research Campus|website=HHMI.org|language=en|access-date=February 2, 2019|date=March 15, 2016}}</ref>  Previously, she was the Chief of the Section on Organelle Biology in the Cell Biology and Metabolism Program, in the Division of Intramural Research in the [[Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development]] at the [[National Institutes of Health]] from 1993 to 2016.  Lippincott-Schwartz received her PhD from [[Johns Hopkins University]], and performed post-doctoral training with Richard Klausner at the NICHD, NIH in Bethesda, Maryland.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last=Davis|first=Tinsley H.|date=July 7, 2009|title=Profile of Jennifer Lippincott-Schwartz|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|language=en|volume=106|issue=27|pages=10881–10883|doi=10.1073/pnas.0905805106|issn=0027-8424|pmid=19567833|pmc=2708775|bibcode=2009PNAS..10610881D|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Lippincott-Schwartz's research revealed that the organelles of [[Eukaryote|eukaryotic cells]] are dynamic, self-organized structures that constantly regenerate themselves through intracellular vesicle traffic, rather than static structures.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last1=Lippincott-Schwartz|first1=J.|last2=Yuan|first2=L.|last3=Tipper|first3=C.|last4=Amherdt|first4=M.|last5=Orci|first5=L.|last6=Klausner|first6=R. D.|date=November 1, 1991|title=Brefeldin A's effects on endosomes, lysosomes, and the TGN suggest a general mechanism for regulating organelle structure and membrane traffic|journal=Cell|volume=67|issue=3|pages=601–616|issn=0092-8674|pmid=1682055|doi=10.1016/0092-8674(91)90534-6|s2cid=2114431}}</ref>  She is also a pioneer in developing live cell imaging techniques to study the dynamic interactions of molecules in cells, including [[photobleaching]] and photoactivation<ref name=":3" /> techniques which allow investigation of subcellular localization, mobility, transport routes, and turnover of important cellular proteins related to membrane trafficking and compartmentalization.  Lippincott-Schwartz's lab also tests mechanistic hypotheses related to protein and organelle functions and dynamics by utilizing quantitative measurements through kinetic modeling and simulation experiments.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://irp.nih.gov/pi/jennifer-lippincott-schwartz|archive-url=https://archive.today/20141130070701/http://irp.nih.gov/pi/jennifer-lippincott-schwartz|archive-date=November 30, 2014|title=Jennifer A. Lippincott-Schwartz, Ph.D.|website=NIH {{!}} Intramural Research Program}}</ref> Along with Craig Blackstone, Lippincott-Schwartz utilized advanced imaging techniques to reveal a more accurate picture of how the peripheral endoplasmic reticulum is structured. Their findings may yield new insights for genetic diseases affecting proteins that help shape the endoplasmic reticulum.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nih.gov/news-events/nih-research-matters/re-envisioning-endoplasmic-reticulum|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170105010338/https://www.nih.gov/news-events/nih-research-matters/re-envisioning-endoplasmic-reticulum|archive-date=January 5, 2017|title=Re-envisioning the endoplasmic reticulum|date=November 7, 2016|work=National Institutes of Health (NIH)|access-date=February 3, 2018|language=en}}</ref> Additionally, Lippincott-Schwartz's laboratory demonstrated that Golgi enzymes constitutively recycle back to the endoplasmic reticulum and that such recycling plays a central role in the maintenance, biogenesis, and inheritance of the Golgi apparatus in mammalian cells.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Sengupta|first1=Prabuddha|last2=Satpute-Krishnan|first2=Prasanna|last3=Seo|first3=Arnold Y.|last4=Burnette|first4=Dylan T.|last5=Patterson|first5=George H.|last6=Lippincott-Schwartz|first6=Jennifer|date=December 8, 2015|title=ER trapping reveals Golgi enzymes continually revisit the ER through a recycling pathway that controls Golgi organization|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|language=en|volume=112|issue=49|pages=E6752–E6761|doi=10.1073/pnas.1520957112|issn=0027-8424|pmid=26598700|pmc=4679030|bibcode=2015PNAS..112E6752S|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Within Lippincott-Schwartz lab, current projects include several cell biological areas.  For example, protein transport and cytoskeleton interaction, organelle assembly and disassembly, and cell polarity generation.  There are also projects analyzing the dynamics of proteins that have been fluorescently labeled.  These proteins are labeled using several live cell imaging techniques such as FRAP, FCS, and photoactivation.<ref>The Marine Biological Laboratory, [http://courses.mbl.edu/physiology/faculty/faculty.html"Meet the Faculty: Jennifer Lippincott-Schwartz"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151228180930/http://courses.mbl.edu/physiology/faculty/faculty.html |date=December 28, 2015 }}, 2011</ref>

Lippincott-Schwartz has dedicated her most recent lab research to photoactivation localization microscopy (PALM), which allows the viewing of molecular distributions of high densities at the nano-scale.<ref name=":1" />

==Early life==
Jennifer Lippincott-Schwartz was born on October 19, 1952, in Manhattan, Kansas.  Her father was a professor of physical chemistry at the [[University of Maryland]]<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Profile of Jennifer Lippincott-Schwartz, Ph.D.|journal = BioTechniques|volume = 40|issue = 4|page = 419|last=Bonetta|first=Laura|date=May 21, 2018|doi=10.2144/06404SP01|pmid = 16629387|doi-access=free}}</ref> and a periodic table could be found hanging in her family's household kitchen.  Lippincott-Schwartz's exposure to her father's work is what sparked her love of science.  The family moved to a farm in Northern Virginia that had several horses and various other animals.  This is where Lippincott-Schwartz found her love of biology.

==Education==

Lippincott-Schwartz attended [[Swarthmore College]], where she majored in psychology and philosophy and graduated with honors from Swarthmore College in 1974.<ref name=":1" /> She taught science at a girl's high school in Kenya for two years before returning to the USA and entering a Master's program in Biology at [[Stanford University]] where she worked on DNA repair in the laboratory of [[Philip Hanawalt]].<ref name=":1" /> She then entered a Biochemistry Ph.D. program at [[Johns Hopkins University]], where she worked in Douglas Fambrough's lab in the Carnegie Institution of Embryology<ref name=":1" /> and studied the dynamics of lysosomal membrane proteins.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lippincott-Schwartz|first1=J.|last2=Fambrough|first2=D.M.|date=May 1, 1986|title=Lysosomal membrane dynamics: structure and interorganellar movement of a major lysosomal membrane glycoprotein.|journal=The Journal of Cell Biology|language=en|volume=102|issue=5|pages=1593–1605|doi=10.1083/jcb.102.5.1593|issn=0021-9525|pmid=2871029|pmc=2114232}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lippincott-Schwartz|first1=J.|last2=Fambrough|first2=D. M.|date=June 5, 1987|title=Cycling of the integral membrane glycoprotein, LEP100, between plasma membrane and lysosomes: kinetic and morphological analysis|journal=Cell|volume=49|issue=5|pages=669–677|issn=0092-8674|pmid=3107839|doi=10.1016/0092-8674(87)90543-5|s2cid=46230310}}</ref>

==Career==

===Postdoctoral work===

After graduating from Johns Hopkins in 1986, Lippincott-Schwartz joined Richard D. Klausner's lab at the [[National Institutes of Health]]. Using the drug [[brefeldin A]] to perturb membrane trafficking, she showed that membranes cycle between the [[endoplasmic reticulum]] and the [[Golgi apparatus|Golgi]],<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lippincott-Schwartz|first1=J.|last2=Yuan|first2=L. C.|last3=Bonifacino|first3=J. S.|last4=Klausner|first4=R. D.|date=March 10, 1989|title=Rapid redistribution of Golgi proteins into the ER in cells treated with brefeldin A: evidence for membrane cycling from Golgi to ER|journal=Cell|volume=56|issue=5|pages=801–813|issn=0092-8674|pmid=2647301|doi=10.1016/0092-8674(89)90685-5|pmc=7173269}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lippincott-Schwartz|first1=J.|last2=Donaldson|first2=J. G.|last3=Schweizer|first3=A.|last4=Berger|first4=E. G.|last5=Hauri|first5=H. P.|last6=Yuan|first6=L. C.|last7=Klausner|first7=R. D.|date=March 9, 1990|title=Microtubule-dependent retrograde transport of proteins into the ER in the presence of brefeldin A suggests an ER recycling pathway|journal=Cell|volume=60|issue=5|pages=821–836|issn=0092-8674|pmid=2178778|doi=10.1016/0092-8674(90)90096-W|s2cid=45505382}}</ref> leading to a recognition that cellular organelles are dynamic, self-organized structures that constantly regenerate themselves through intracellular vesicle traffic.<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lippincott-Schwartz|first1=J.|last2=Donaldson|first2=J. G.|last3=Klausner|first3=R. D.|date=March 1, 1992|title=Brefeldin A: insights into the control of membrane traffic and organelle structure.|journal=The Journal of Cell Biology|language=en|volume=116|issue=5|pages=1071–1080|doi=10.1083/jcb.116.5.1071|issn=0021-9525|pmid=1740466|pmc=2289364}}</ref>

===NIH===

Lippincott-Schwartz became a staff fellow at the [[National Institute of Child Health and Human Development]] at NIH in 1990.  During this time, Lippincott-Schwartz began developing techniques to use [[green fluorescent protein]] (GFP) to visualize cellular trafficking pathways in living cells.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Presley|first1=J. F.|last2=Cole|first2=N. B.|last3=Schroer|first3=T. A.|last4=Hirschberg|first4=K.|last5=Zaal|first5=K. J.|last6=Lippincott-Schwartz|first6=J.|date=September 4, 1997|title=ER-to-Golgi transport visualized in living cells|journal=Nature|volume=389|issue=6646|pages=81–85|doi=10.1038/38001|issn=0028-0836|pmid=9288971|bibcode=1997Natur.389...81P|s2cid=5467632}}</ref> She refined the technique of [[fluorescence recovery after photobleaching]] (FRAP) to use in studying the dynamics of membrane proteins.  In this method, GFP-tagged membrane proteins are subjected to photobleaching in a small area of the cell, and then the cell is imaged to discover how long it takes for non-bleached proteins to replace the bleached ones, i.e. how long it takes for the fluorescence to recover. Before this work, it was thought that the membrane proteins in organelles such as the ER, Golgi, and plasma membrane were fixed in place.  However, the FRAP technique proved that molecules within cells move quite rapidly and are able to diffuse freely.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Cole|first1=N. B.|last2=Smith|first2=C. L.|last3=Sciaky|first3=N.|last4=Terasaki|first4=M.|last5=Edidin|first5=M.|last6=Lippincott-Schwartz|first6=J.|date=August 9, 1996|title=Diffusional mobility of Golgi proteins in membranes of living cells|journal=Science|volume=273|issue=5276|pages=797–801|issn=0036-8075|pmid=8670420|doi=10.1126/science.273.5276.797|bibcode=1996Sci...273..797C|s2cid=9426667|url=http://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/e945/88996d101f847819c3286bd4ed1db9519f7f.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190308002658/http://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/e945/88996d101f847819c3286bd4ed1db9519f7f.pdf|archive-date=March 8, 2019}}</ref>  Lippincott-Schwartz subsequently introduced photoactivatable GFP that increases its fluorescence after irradiation.<ref name=":3">{{cite journal|last1=Patterson|first1=G. H.|title=A Photoactivatable GFP for Selective Photolabeling of Proteins and Cells|journal=Science|volume=297|issue=5588|year=2002|pages=1873–1877|issn=0036-8075|doi=10.1126/science.1074952|pmid=12228718|bibcode=2002Sci...297.1873P|s2cid=45058411}}</ref> This allowed Lippincott-Schwartz and her post-doc George Patterson to track the transport of cargo molecules through the Golgi with great precision,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Patterson|first1=George H.|last2=Hirschberg|first2=Koret|last3=Polishchuk|first3=Roman S.|last4=Gerlich|first4=Daniel|last5=Phair|first5=Robert D.|last6=Lippincott-Schwartz|first6=Jennifer|date=June 13, 2008|title=Transport through the Golgi apparatus by rapid partitioning within a two-phase membrane system|journal=Cell|volume=133|issue=6|pages=1055–1067|doi=10.1016/j.cell.2008.04.044|issn=1097-4172|pmc=2481404|pmid=18555781}}</ref> leading to the realization that cargo transport is not an ordered sequential process; instead, the apparently separate membranous stacks of the Golgi are a single continuous structure, and proteins rapidly equilibrate through the layers.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Simon|first=Sanford M.|date=June 13, 2008|title=Golgi governance: the third way|journal=Cell|volume=133|issue=6|pages=951–953|doi=10.1016/j.cell.2008.05.037|issn=1097-4172|pmc=2711685|pmid=18555771}}</ref>

Lippincott-Schwartz's work on photoactivatable GFP led to a collaboration with [[Eric Betzig]] of [[Howard Hughes Medical Institute]]'s [[Janelia Farm Research Campus]] in which the ability to turn GFP fluorescence on and off was used to develop one of the first "superresolution imaging" technologies, photoactivation localization microscopy ([[Photoactivated localization microscopy|PALM]]).<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Betzig|first1=E.|last2=Patterson|first2=G. H.|last3=Sougrat|first3=R.|last4=Lindwasser|first4=O. W.|last5=Olenych|first5=S.|last6=Bonifacino|first6=J. S.|last7=Davidson|first7=M. W.|last8=Lippincott-Schwartz|first8=J.|last9=Hess|first9=H. F.|title=Imaging Intracellular Fluorescent Proteins at Nanometer Resolution|journal=Science|volume=313|issue=5793|year=2006|pages=1642–1645|issn=0036-8075|doi=10.1126/science.1127344|pmid=16902090|bibcode=2006Sci...313.1642B|s2cid=807611|doi-access=free}}</ref> The development of "super-resolved fluorescence microscopy" was recognized in 2014 by the award of the Nobel Prize in Chemistry to Eric Betzig along with William E. Moerner of Stanford University, and Stefan W. Hell of Max Planck Institute for Biophysical Chemistry.<ref>{{Cite web| last = The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences| title = Scientific Background on the Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2014: Super-Resolved Fluorescence Microscopy| access-date = April 20, 2015| date = October 8, 2014| url = https://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/chemistry/laureates/2014/advanced-chemistryprize2014.pdf}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web| title = NIH Grantee Honored With 2014 Nobel Prize in Chemistry: Early prototype microscope built at NIH| work = National Institute of Health: Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (NICHD)| access-date = April 20, 2015| date = October 8, 2014| url = https://www.nichd.nih.gov/newsroom/releases/100814-NIH-grantee-Nobel}}</ref>

Lippincott-Schwartz has used PALM to assess the stoichiometry and composition of membrane receptors<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Renz|first1=Malte|last2=Daniels|first2=Brian R.|last3=Vámosi|first3=György|last4=Arias|first4=Irwin M.|last5=Lippincott-Schwartz|first5=Jennifer|date=October 30, 2012|title=Plasticity of the asialoglycoprotein receptor deciphered by ensemble FRET imaging and single-molecule counting PALM imaging|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America|volume=109|issue=44|pages=E2989–2997|doi=10.1073/pnas.1211753109|issn=1091-6490|pmc=3497821|pmid=23043115|doi-access=free}}</ref> and has collaborated with Vladislav Verkhusha of [[Albert Einstein College of Medicine]] in New York to develop two-color PALM.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Subach|first1=Fedor V|last2=Patterson|first2=George H|last3=Manley|first3=Suliana|author-link3=Suliana Manley|last4=Gillette|first4=Jennifer M|last5=Lippincott-Schwartz|first5=Jennifer|last6=Verkhusha|first6=Vladislav V|year=2009|title=Photoactivatable mCherry for high-resolution two-color fluorescence microscopy|journal=Nature Methods|volume=6|issue=2|pages=153–159|doi=10.1038/nmeth.1298|issn=1548-7091|pmc=2901231|pmid=19169259}}</ref> She used a combination of five super-resolution techniques to show that the [[endoplasmic reticulum]] is composed of a dense tubular matrix, instead of the sheets seen at lower resolution.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lippincott-Schwartz|first1=Jennifer|last2=Blackstone|first2=Craig|last3=Betzig|first3=Eric|last4=Hess|first4=Harald F.|last5=Harvey|first5=Kirsten|last6=Pasolli|first6=H. Amalia|last7=Xu|first7=C. Shan|last8=Legant|first8=Wesley R.|last9=Li|first9=Dong|date=October 28, 2016|title=Increased spatiotemporal resolution reveals highly dynamic dense tubular matrices in the peripheral ER|journal=Science|language=en|volume=354|issue=6311|article-number=aaf3928|doi=10.1126/science.aaf3928|issn=0036-8075|pmid=27789813|pmc=6528812}}</ref>

===Janelia Research Campus===

In 2016, Lippincott-Schwartz moved from NIH to the [[Janelia Research Campus]] of the [[Howard Hughes Medical Institute]] to initiate the Neuronal Cell Biology Program at Janelia.<ref name=":0" />
